newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-BoPs, price indexes imply GDP detraction.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-BoPs, price indexes imply GDP detraction.

text.p: December quarter import and export price data and the monthly balance of payments data together suggest a small detraction from Australian quarterly GDP growth of 0.2 or 0.3 percentage points.
Three pieces of information are needed to calculate the net export figure: the original trade data, seasonality and price movements.

The original trade flows are in the latest monthly current account releases, the seasonality can be taken (with some caution) from the previous December quarter balance of payments and the best indication for price movements is in the monthly import and export price indexes.

With the December price indexes, issued today, we now have as much information as we are going to get until the issue of the December quarter balance of payments itself on March 4, the day before GDP.
For example, original merchandise exports in October, November and December add up to A$19.603 billion.

In 1995, Q4 original exports were 103.7 percent of seasonally adjusted exports. If we assume that the same relationship holds true this year then the latest December quarter seasonally adjusted exports will be A$18.912 billion.
This is a big assumption but there is little alternative: one cannot add up the monthly seasonally adjusted export numbers because the monthly and quarterly adjustment can very different.
Our seasonally adjusted number has to be adjusted for price movements by dividing by a December quarter price deflator.

That figure is not available but in the September quarter the deflator was 93.1 percent. The export price index (covering goods and services) fell 2.0 percent, suggesting a December deflator of 91.2 percent.
Adjusting the current-price estimate with the new deflator gives an estimate for December quarter constant-price, seasonally adjusted exports of A$20.737 billion.

Since that is A$587 million or 0.5 percent of GDP greater than the September quarter result, it implies a contribution from merchandise exports to quarterly growth in the expenditure-based GDP estimate (GDP-E) of 0.5 percentage points.
The same process produces a zero contribution from services credits, minus 0.7 percentage points from merchandise imports and minus 0.1 points from services debits.
The bottom line is a fall in net exports of A$20 million, implying a detraction of 0.2 percentage points (more precisely: 0.25 percentage points).

Macquarie Bank economist Andrew Ticehurst said: "We expect export volumes to rise by around two percent, led by manufacturing exports but import volumes should rise by around three percent, mainly reflecting imports of intermediate (productive but not capital) goods.Z "This implies a negative contribution from net exports of around 0.2 percentage points." (c) Reuters Limited 1997
